messages.subject: optimizing code
parts:
Hi

I have been working in a change point model. The model works fine for simulated data, the attach R code generates simulated data and run stan. But when i run this model on real data, it doesnt converged even after 5 hours running 15000 iterations on 4 chains.

I would very much appreciate your help to find a way to optimize this code, and run faster.

I have read that you dont recomend the use iof inverse wishart for variance, but i havent been able to apply the lkj_corr distribution properly.

mod <- "
data{
int n;
int parmt;
int nsubj;
real y[n];
int id[n];
real x[n];
vector[parmt] pm;
cov_matrix[parmt] prec;
cov_matrix[parmt] R;
}

parameters {
vector[parmt] b[nsubj];
vector[parmt] mub;
real<lower=0> sigma_y;
cov_matrix[parmt] sigma2;
}

model{

for (j in 1:nsubj){
b[j] ~ multi_normal(mub, sigma2);
}

sigma_y ~ uniform(0,200);

for (i in 1:n){
real mu;
mu <- b[id[i],1] + b[id[i],2] * x[i] + (b[id[i],3] * ((x[i] - b[id[i],4]) * int_step(x[i]-b[id[i],4])));
y[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma_y);
}

mub ~ multi_normal(pm, prec);

sigma2 ~ inv_wishart(parmt, R);
}"

Thank you

-- Mauricio

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] optimizing code
parts:
I'd recommend more informative priors.

Unless you expect parameters to have values like 500,
a normal(0,200) prior's essentially flat. This can
cause problems with convergence if the data are
separable, and also just cause slow mixing.

The following probably isn't your big bottleneck compared
to the multivariate distributions, but you can speed up:

for (i in 1:n){
real mu;
mu <- b[id[i],1] + b[id[i],2] * x[i] + (b[id[i],3] * ((x[i] - b[id[i],4]) * int_step(x[i]-b[id[i],4])));
y[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma_y);
}

by vectorizing the normal call with:

{
real mu[n];
for (i in 1:n)
mu[i] <- b[id[i],1]

y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}

The brackets are there so that mu[n] is a local variable.

Rather than the old BUGS-style int-step function, if-then is more
efficient as it doesn't do any unnecessary evaluations. So that'd
be:

mu[i] <- b[id[i],1] + b[id[i],2] * x[i];
if (x[i] > b[id[i],4])
mu[i] <- mu[i] + (b[id[i],3] * ((x[i] - b[id[i],4])

(Note that I changed the condition to remove an extra subtraction;
this wont' matter if x and b are both data, but if either is a parameter,
the way I wrote it will be faster.)

For the LKJ model, check out page 95 of the Stan 1.3
manual.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] optimizing code
parts:
I don't see any reason the LKJ version would be a problem
if the inverse wishart works.

Ben will have a better idea of what's going on with the LKJ
prior than me.


One issue might be the fat priors you have on Sigma_sd:

Sigma_sd ~ cauchy(0,5);

Are you expecting it to be potentially large? If not, you could
try smaller values.


Another thing you need to do is ensure that parameter
constraints match the support of their sampling distributions.
A parameter declared like this:

real<lower=0> sigma_y;

shouldn't be used like this:

sigma_y ~ uniform(0,50);


You need to declare sigma_y as:

real<lower=0,upper=50> sigma_y;

Having said that, I wouldn't use such fat priors on
sigma_y unless you expect values of it that high.
And although it's almost trivial to execute, you
don't need the uniform sampling statement if sigma_y
is declared with upper and lower bounds.


Another thing that worries me in the model is this
data declaration:

cov_matrix[parmt] prec;

and this usage:

mub ~ multi_normal(pm, prec);

Our multi_normal parameterization uses covariance matrices,
not precision matrices. But that matches what you did
in the Wishart example, so I doubt that's your underlying
problem.

- Bob

vector<lower=0,upper=20>[parmt] Sigma_sd;

}
}
}

The differences that i was having between the wishart and lkj models were because of a missipecification on the scale matrix of the inv_wishart.

Once i included more informative priors (o less non-informative) it also worked faster.

So, as i understand, for standard deviations it is recomended to use cauchy(0,1), instead of a uniform(), right?

So, you can fix it, there is a typo in the stan manual (1.3), in page 95, for the correation example, the line:
Sigma[m,m] <- sigma[m] * sigma[m] * Omega[m,n];

should be
Sigma[m,m] <- sigma[m] * sigma[m] * Omega[m,m];

Using the lkj approach to estimate the correlation matrix and standard deviations, i get one weird result in for the Rhat, for 
Sigma_corr[1,1] I get an Rhat = NaN

all the other Rhats are 1, I guess is because it is in the diagaonal of the correlation matrix, but for the other elements of the diagonla I get Rhat=1. I dont think this is a problem, but is weird.

Thanks a lot for your help


The code that works fine is the follow

data{
int n;
int parmt;
int nsubj;
real y[n];
int id[n];
real x[n];
vector[parmt] pm;
cov_matrix[parmt] cov_v;

}

parameters {
vector[parmt] b[nsubj];
vector[parmt] mub;

real<lower=0,upper=20> sigma_y;
corr_matrix[parmt] Sigma_corr;
vector<lower=0,upper=20>[parmt] Sigma_sd;

}

transformed parameters {
cov_matrix[parmt] Sigma; // covariance matrix
for (m in 1:parmt) {
Sigma[m,m] <- Sigma_sd[m] * Sigma_sd[m] * Sigma_corr[m,m];
for (k in (m+1):parmt) {
Sigma[m,k] <- Sigma_sd[m] * Sigma_sd[k] * Sigma_corr[m,k];
Sigma[k,m] <- Sigma[m,k];
}
}
}

model{

Sigma_sd ~ cauchy(0,1);

Sigma_corr ~ lkj_corr(2.0);

for (j in 1:nsubj){
b[j] ~ multi_normal(mub, Sigma);
}

{
real mu[n];
for (i in 1:n){
mu[i] <- b[id[i],1] + b[id[i],2] * x[i];
if (x[i] > b[id[i],4])
mu[i] <- mu[i] + (b[id[i],3] * (x[i] - b[id[i],4]));
}
y ~ normal(mu, sigma_y);
}
mub ~ multi_normal(pm, cov_v);

}
